title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
subject: histoire
description: On **August 6, 1945**, an atomic bomb flattened Hiroshima. Three days later, Nagasaki. The Second World War ended, and the nuclear age began.

hero.hook: In a flash brighter than a thousand suns, an entire city disappears.

blocks.text: On **August 6, 1945**, at **8:15** in the morning, the sky over **Hiroshima**, a Japanese city, caught fire. In one instant, a single bomb killed between **70,000 and 80,000** people. Three days later, **Nagasaki** met the same fate.
These strikes ended the war in Asia and opened the **nuclear age**: for the first time, humanity held a weapon able to destroy itself.

A letter from Albert Einstein, written with the physicist [[Leó Szilárd]], pushed Washington to act out of fear of a Nazi bomb. In **1942**, the United States launched the **Manhattan Project**: about **130,000** people and **2 billion** dollars. Secret sites went up at Oak Ridge, Hanford and Los Alamos.

blocks.caption: The Trinity test, July 16, 1945: the first nuclear explosion

blocks.text: The **Trinity** test, in the [[Jornada del Muerto]] desert of New Mexico, was so powerful that people more than **150 km** away thought they saw the sun rise twice.

On **July 16, 1945**, the **Trinity** test succeeded. **Robert Oppenheimer**, the scientific director of the project, thought of a line from the Mahabharata, an ancient Indian text: “Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.”

When Franklin Roosevelt died, the new American president **Harry Truman** learned that the bomb existed. Germany had surrendered, but Japan fought on, notably with the [[kamikazes]], pilots who threw their planes at Allied ships. An invasion of Japan might cost **500,000 to a million** American casualties.
Hiroshima had been deliberately spared from conventional raids, so that the effects of a single nuclear explosion could be measured precisely.

At [[Potsdam]], an Allied conference in July 1945, tension with the USSR was rising. Using the bomb also meant putting American power on display. Hiroshima was chosen for its military role and for the bowl of hills around it, which would concentrate the blast.

On **August 6**, the bomber **Enola Gay** dropped **Little Boy** on Hiroshima. Up to **140,000** people were dead by the end of the year, from burns and from [[Radiation sickness (acute radiation syndrome)]]. On **August 9**, the [[Bockscar]] aimed first at [[Kokura]], but clouds sent it on to **Nagasaki**. The **Fat Man** bomb exploded.

blocks.caption: The mushroom cloud over Hiroshima, August 6, 1945

blocks.text: **Tsutomu Yamaguchi** survived both bombs: hurt at Hiroshima on the 6th, he went home to Nagasaki, where he still was on August 9.

That same day, the [[Soviet invasion of Manchuria (August 9, 1945)]] destroyed any hope of Soviet mediation. On **August 15**, Emperor **Hirohito** announced the surrender on the radio, in the [[Gyokuon-hōsō]], a historic broadcast.

sections.title: The long shadow of the atom

blocks.text: The survivors, the [[Hibakusha]], carry cancers, scars and an ethical debate that never ends. Geopolitically, the age of [[Nuclear deterrence]] began: threatening to use the bomb so that the other side never attacks. The Cold War opened. Hiroshima remains the harshest warning about science placed at the service of destruction.

events.title: Nagasaki and the USSR
events.detail: Fat Man dropped, and the Soviets entered the war.

blocks.text: **Hiroshima**, **August 6, 1945**: tens of thousands dead in one instant. After Nagasaki, Japan surrendered, and the nuclear age began.
